| `attachable/scripts` | partial | `pre_animation` runs first every frame, and its assignments are what the `animate` conditions read - evaluating them the other way round leaves every `v.` at zero, which answers "no" to every question a pack asks about itself. An `animate` entry's Molang expression is a BLEND AMOUNT, not a condition: SC-180 section 4.1.1. Every condition in the surveyed corpus is a comparison answering zero or one, so this is indistinguishable there and differs for vanilla's own entries, which blend a walk by `query.modified_move_speed`. An entry naming an animation CONTROLLER rather than an animation runs it - SC-180 section 5 - unless the controller is one the add-on does not ship, which is the case for the two attachables naming Mojang's `controller.animation.elytra.default`. An animation's clock is the HOLDER's, starting the first frame that entry's blend is non-zero and running from then on whatever the blend does. `scripts.initialize`, `scripts.scale` and `scripts.variables` are still not read. SC-180 section 4.1.1. |
| `attachable/item` | partial | An attachable is keyed by the identifier of the item it dresses and a pack may name one it did not define. An add-on item binds under its logical identifier; a vanilla one binds under its own registry name, which is what such a stack already carries. A stack is asked for its logical identity first and for its registry name only in its absence, so a carrier item whose content is unbound can never fall through to a vanilla binding. Nothing is registered either way. A vanilla item's attachable is drawn in THIRD PERSON ONLY, and that is measured rather than chosen: a probe on `minecraft:stick` with an unconditional `scripts.animate` was drawn in third person by a Bedrock client and not at all in first, and a later probe on a custom item held the same way with the same bones WAS drawn in first person - so vanilla-versus-custom is the isolated variable. The corpus's one such pack writes four first-person animations Bedrock never plays, and this build does not play them either. The item therefore keeps drawing itself in first person, and its item definition is replaced with one blanking the two third-person hand contexts alone - against the four an add-on item blanks, where the hand hook draws instead. That replacement is served in the `minecraft` namespace, which is what a Bedrock pack does to a vanilla item. Vanilla's own definition is WRAPPED rather than rewritten: it is read out of the game's jar and its `model` carried across verbatim as the fallback, so a bow's condition over `using_item` and the range dispatch beneath it, a potion's tint and a compass's needle all survive untouched. A definition that cannot be read is not replaced at all - no override is written, the attachable still draws, the flat sprite draws with it, and SCE-2042 says so. An add-on may change how an item is drawn; it may not cost the item its behaviour. An attachable naming an identifier that is neither a pack's item nor a registered one resolves to nothing and reports SCE-2041. The pack that also replaces such an item's ICON does it by writing over the vanilla texture path, which is `rp-textures` and not this entry. |
| `attachable/first_person` | partial | It does need its own path, and the reason is not that hand rendering is awkward: Bedrock does not draw an attachable at the hand at all. It poses it in PLAYER space, which in first person is a space the game never draws in, because no player model is submitted. So the space is rebuilt against the camera, and the order that survives measurement is the short one: the origin is dropped to the feet by the player's own eye height, read per frame, and NOTHING is rotated. Two Bedrock screenshots, one pitched fully up and one fully down, put the character's parts in the same screen positions - so the model rides the camera, and undoing the camera was tried and had to come out. AN EARLIER VERSION OF THIS NOTE DESCRIBED AN IMPLEMENTATION THAT NO LONGER EXISTS. It explained the space as undoing the camera's pitch and its yaw-over-body, and it justified the order of the steps by a 1.62 sin(pitch) error that ordering would have caused. All of that was removed with the rotation it described. Read this paragraph, not that one. The scale is the part with no measurement behind it. First person multiplies by the 0.9375 a player model carries, written out by hand because nothing in the first-person pass supplies it, and the reason recorded in the source is that the model was "6.7% larger than the same model on the same player seen from outside". That reason is the premise the rotation work above refuted - first person is not the player's space, so its size is not the third-person size - and the constant outlived the diagnosis, the same way a mirror once did. Two paired captures of the corpus's body-parented character put its head visibly LARGER on the Bedrock client than here, by more than 6.7%, so removing the constant is not known to be the whole of it and is not known to be right either. It needs its own frame. A worn attachable is not drawn in first person. The seam is the hand render, which is offered the two hands and nothing else; the four armour slots reach the third-person layer only. A halo sits above and behind the eye and would be invisible anyway, but an armour attachable that reaches in front of the player is a real omission rather than a hidden one. WHAT IS CONFIRMED, and what is not, was re-measured against a pair of captures rather than inherited. Confirmed: the channel composition (independent channels, translation outermost **within one bone**, SC-180 section 4.1.3), that a conditional entry fires (section 4.4), that the wearer's `body` carries a half turn in first person (section 4.2.1), and that a model in this build lands where the offline survey says it does - the survey's own numbers predict this build's head centre at 20% of screen width and the capture puts it at 20%, so the instrument is good to about 1.5% and the numbers below it can be believed. **THE COMPOSITION ACROSS THE PACK/WEARER BOUNDARY IS NOW MEASURED, AND IT WAS WRONG.** The wearer's transform goes outside the pack's - `wearer x pack`, so the pack's `position` is applied INSIDE the wearer's rotation, not after it. It was the other way round, and the corpus's `.hand` is the one animation in the surveyed set that writes onto a bone the wearer drives (`position [0,-1,-6]` onto the cube-less `body`), which is why the sign flipped on the one character that was wrong and left the other untouched. Probe v13 (`probe11`..`probe13`): a bone named `body` carrying `position [0,0,-24]` and no animation of its own, read in both views. Third person lands at z -24 either way - **the wearer's transform is ~identity there, so the order is invisible from third person** - and first person lands at z +24, the bar out of sight behind the camera. Correcting it moves the `body`-parented character's first-person `body2` from z -12.08..-3.09 to z -0.08..8.91, and leaves the `waist`-parented one byte-for-byte unchanged. **SC-180 section 4.2.2** records the frame and what v11 got wrong on the way to it. **A PARENT'S ANIMATION ROTATION CARRIES ITS CHILD'S POSITION — MEASURED, probe v16, and it is what this build does.** v12 and v14 asked this and answered it both ways; both rigs were broken (v12 asked the reader to compare two bars that do not both exist under one of the readings, and v14/v15 asked a depth question of a third-person camera). v16 rotates about Z so the answer is *up or sideways* and came out sideways. **SC-180 section 4.2.3.** **EVERY HALO IN THE CORPUS WAS INVISIBLE, AND IT WAS THE FACE CHOICE.** Both characters declare their halo identically - `size [12,0,10]` at `uv [-10,54]` - and neither drew it. The two faces' rectangles are not interchangeable: the one this build drew measures **0% alpha** across the shipped textures and the one it dropped carries a **22%/18% ring**. A quad is invisible when the rectangle it samples is transparent, which is not the same as being back-facing, so the long- standing justification for dropping either face was a statement about geometry that said nothing about visibility. Drawing the POSITIVE face on each axis fixes it; **only the height axis was changed**, because the depth axis is pinned by probe v17 and the width axis is **unmeasured**. **SC-180 section 4.2.4.** Blockbench settles what an offline alpha scan could not: the texture and model were never in question, only the face this build chose. **THE EYES FLICKERED BECAUSE TWO OF THEIR QUADS SHARE A PLANE.** `eye2` #0 with #1 and #3 with #4 are each coplanar at z 1.98 and overlap 0.90 x 3.00, with **different rectangles**, so the fight is one eye part's texture against another's - and it is visible only in the third-person front view, which is the only view an eye decal is visible from. Fixed by walking each flat quad off its own surface in declaration order. **The three failed attempts and their single cause are the transferable part: both spaces are reflections, so a normal taken after the space conversion faces the opposite way** (measured: model space `(0,0,-1)`, converted `(0,0,+1)`), and every attempt using one pushed the decal INTO its surface. The step is a fortieth of the gap the corpus leaves between an eye and a face, so it is derived rather than fitted. **SC-180 section 4.2.5.** The render type's own Z-offset layer was also removed, on the measurement that doing so made the flicker better - it was applied and pulling the wrong way. **A CROUCHING PLAYER MOVED THE WHOLE CHARACTER 0.35 BLOCKS UP, IN FIRST PERSON ONLY.** Two causes, both a Minecraft implementation detail passed as though the engine had asked for it, both now measured against the Bedrock client: - **the first-person ORIGIN read the live `getEyeHeight()`** (SC-180 section 3.4.2). It reads   well - a crouched player's eye is lower, so a constant would sink with them - and it is what   this build did. The engine's first-person attachable is anchored to the **player**, not to the   camera looking at it, and **Bedrock moves nothing on a crouch**. The constant   `AttachableSpace.STANDING_EYE_HEIGHT` already existed and already documented itself as "the   value for a player standing still". - **the third-person wearer skeleton read a Java `ModelPart`'s POSITION** (SC-180 section   4.2.1). That position is not zero whenever the player is not standing still - crouching moves   `body` and `head` along Y - and the engine's wearer bones are written as **rotations** only.   **Rotation only now.**  **THE SHIELD IS THE LAST UNRESOLVED ITEM, and no rule accounts for it.** With every composition rule measured and matching - own channel order (v9/v10), parent animation rotation carrying a child's position (v16), parent declared rotation carrying (v14), the wearer boundary (v13), the flat-cube face choice (v17 + Blockbench), the UV normalisation (v18) and the coplanar decal separation - there is **no rule-level explanation left for it**. Attribution on `kivotos:hoshino_onbu`, first person, deleting one `.hand` entry at a time: \| removed from `.hand` \| `bag2` top \| drop \| \|---\|---\|---\| \| nothing \| 34.43 \| - \| \| `leftArm2` `rotation [87.5,-85,-47.5]` \| 27.71 \| **6.72** \| \| `bag2` `position [0,1,1]` \| 33.04 \| 1.39 \| So **83 % of it is the arm's animation rotation** - `leftArm2` reaches a net roll of -95 degrees (idle -35, `.hand` -47.5, bind -12.5) - and the rest is the shield's own position. Both are the pack author's own numbers, authored against the engine, and this build now applies them by rules the probes show agree with it. **Two readings remain and neither has been taken.** Either an unmeasured rule still exists, or this is a sub-block residual whose magnitude this document does not claim to know. §3.4.4's standing decision is **not to chase sub-block residuals with fitted constants**, and five have died in this area - every one standing in for a rule that had not been measured. **Six rules HAVE now been measured, and none of them is this**, which is itself the finding. **What is needed next is another probe, not another constant.** **Probe v20 is built and awaiting a Bedrock frame** (`probe20`, 100 % original, one item and two marker bones). It asks the one remaining unmeasured pair that survives being asked as "up or sideways": **does a bone's OWN DECLARED rotation carry that same bone's animation position?** - which is exactly `bag2`, a declared rotation plus a `.hand` position of `[0,1,1]`. This build already does carry it (`BoneMatrices.local` composes `T(pivot) · R_declared · (T_anim · R_anim · S_anim) · T(-pivot)`), and the survey confirms the rig lands sideways: `m_bind x 23..25, y -4..4` against a reference cube at the origin, in both views. Nothing about the claim above changes until a frame arrives; if it comes back "up", the rule is wrong for every attachable with a declared rotation and an animated position, and the numbers quoted in this file have to be re-taken rather than adjusted. The pair SC-180 section 4.2.6 proposes for this - a child offset **along** the axis its parent's roll turns - **cannot be asked at all**, and the reason is arithmetic rather than engineering: a rotation about Z leaves `(0,0,N)` where it is, so "carries" and "does not carry" place the offset in the same place for every angle. That is the same shape as the four mis-designed rigs (v12, v14, v15, v19), so the pair was not used and section 4.2.6 was left alone. The second unmeasured pair - a bone's declared rotation against its own ANIMATION rotation, i.e. the order `R_bind · R_anim` - is deliberately untouched: with a roll bind and a yaw animation both candidates land pointing **up** and differ only in depth, which is the third-person camera's weakest axis and the reason v14 and v15 died. NOT confirmed, and now contradicted: the claim that the character appears "face visible, on both clients". On the same pair of captures her face is visible on the Bedrock client and NOT here. The head's net rotation about Y is what decides that, and this build's is 180 (wearer) plus -85 (`root2`, the pack's own first-person animation) plus -25 (`head2`) = +70 degrees, so she is turned away. No combination of the two wearer's half turns and either sign of the pack's own angles reaches zero, which is what a face-on head needs - so the difference is not the wearer's half turn and has not been located. The bone rotation order (SC-180 section 4.2) is NOT the cause either, and that was worth knowing: all six orders were computed over the real rig and every one of them leaves the head turned away, the whole extents moving by under half a block. A rig whose head chain turns about one axis at a time cannot testify about the order, and this one cannot be fixed by choosing among them. Both clients draw this pass with a fixed projection that ignores the FOV setting (measured), and the difference between those two fixed projections is not a vertical 60-versus-70: scaling camera-space x and y by tan(35)/tan(30) - the correction that premise derives - made the matched character visibly worse. Five fitted constants and one derived one have died on this residual, and a sixth will not be found by fitting. The survey is the instrument that does not fit, and what it needs next is a probe carrying a gauge of known length, so that size and distance arrive as numbers instead of as a comparison of two silhouettes. `:testkit:survey` can now answer the two-view question in one run (`attachable.<id> compare`): which entries of `scripts.animate` resolved in each view, what each condition evaluated to, whether each animation can draw at all, and each bone's facing and scale. The last two are properties of the POSE and so compare across views, which the extents do not - those are in each view's own space, and putting them in one space needs a player yaw an offline tool does not have and will not invent. Run against the corpus's two characters it separates them in a single cell: the `waist`-parented one's first-person animation reads a blend of 1.00 and DRAWS NOTHING, because it is a zero-length `loop: true` that ends on every frame, while the `body`-parented one's reads the same 1.00 and draws. Every bone of the first poses identically in both views; every bone of the second differs. **That is the whole of the difference between a character that is right in both views and one that is not, and it is the `loop` rule of SC-180 section 4.1 - not a coordinate space, not a projection, and not a constant.** The one open question this leaves is whether the Bedrock client applies that second character's zero-length `hold_on_last_frame` at all, because if it does not she would sit at bind-plus-idle there, her head facing the viewer, which is what the capture shows. That is a question about the engine, not about a number to add. Three of the corpus's attachables name vanilla's `controller.animation.elytra.default` in `scripts.animate` and no pack ships it, so this build resolves the entry to nothing and prints it unresolved in BOTH views. Checked against Mojang's own file rather than assumed: the controller's states play the bare short names `default`, `gliding`, `sneaking`, `sleeping` and `swimming`, and short names resolve against the attachable's own `animations` map, which defines none of those five for this item - so it is inert here, and its absence cannot be the first-person difference. **The general gap is real, though, and worth naming: this build has no vanilla animation namespace at all, so a pack naming a vanilla animation or animation controller silently loses it.** That is a missing-implementation category rather than a bug, and nothing in the ledger records it. |
| `attachable/worn` | partial | A worn attachable reaches the render layer only because the stack's minecraft:equippable names an equipment asset. Vanilla filters what it puts on the render state - HumanoidMobRenderer.getEquipmentIfRenderable asks HumanoidArmorLayer.shouldRender, which asks assetId().isPresent() - so a stack without one leaves headEquipment and its three neighbours empty and the layer is handed nothing at all. The asset named is ours and draws nothing: it declares a single layer of a type no humanoid renders, because the codec rejects an empty layer map and any type a humanoid DOES render would put a flat armour piece over the model. This lives on the STACK, so a stack made by an older build carries an equippable without the asset and stays invisible until it is made again (SC-120 section 5). That is a real upgrade hazard, not only a development one. Vanilla's CustomHeadLayer still draws the item's own flat model on the head, beside the attachable. Bedrock shows only the attachable. |
